papers.title: Effects of a standardized saffron extract (Safr'Inside™) on menopause-related symptoms: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in perimenopausal women
papers.abstract: Menopausal symptoms, which may emerge during perimenopause and include psychological, somatic, vasomotor, and sleep-related disturbances, can substantially impair women's well-being and quality of life. Saffron (Crocus sativus L.) has emerged as a promising non-hormonal nutritional approach, with potential benefits for emotional wellbeing and stress-related symptoms. This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of Safr'Inside, a standardized saffron extract, in perimenopausal women. This multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 104 healthy perimenopausal women (mean age: 45.7 {+/-} 3.7 years) receiving Safr'Inside (30 mg/day) or matched placebo for 12 weeks. Assessments were performed at baseline, 6 week, and 12 weeks. The primary outcome was change in menopausal symptom severity assessed using the Greene Climacteric Scale (GCS). Secondary outcomes included mood assessed using the Profile of Mood States (POMS), sleep quality using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and health-related quality of life using the Short Form-36(SF-36). Metabolic, endocrine, and safety parameters were also assessed. At week 12, total GCS scores decreased significantly more with Safr'Inside than with placebo, with mean reductions of 68% and 17%, respectively (p<0.0001). Improvements were already evident at week 6 and were most pronounced for psychological and somatic symptoms, including anxiety and depression. Night sweats significantly improved, while the overall vasomotor score showed a favourable trend (p=0.06). Saffron also improved negative mood, selected sleep-related outcomes and several dimensions of quality of life. Safr'Inside significantly reduced overall perimenopausal symptom burden, with benefits across psychological, somatic, mood, sleep-related, and selected vasomotor outcomes. These findings support further investigation of standardized saffron extract as a non-hormonal nutritional approach for perimenopausal symptom management.

papers.title: Glymphatic Dysfunction Across Sleep Disorders and Its Cognitive Implications
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), sleep deprivation (SD), and narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), are associated with cognitive dysfunction and an increased risk of neurodegenerative disease. Glymphatic transport disruption has been suggested as one potential mechanistic link. However, evidence across sleep disorders and glymphatic-related metrics remains fragmented. We aimed to determine whether glymphatic-related metrics are altered in OSA, SD, and NT1. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical and preclinical studies to determine whether glymphatic-related metrics are altered in OSA, SD, and NT1. Across studies of OSA, glymphatic-related metrics indicated significant impairment of glymphatic transport with a moderate negative association between apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) and diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index (r=-0.53, 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.63 to -0.41; p<0.001). Available evidence did not demonstrate statistically significant alterations in glymphatic measures in SD or NT1. These findings suggest that impaired glymphatic transport may represent a potential pathway linking OSA to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative risk. However, current evidence is insufficient to determine whether comparable alterations occur in SD or NT1. Substantial heterogeneity across studies highlights the need for standardized reporting and harmonized methodologies to advance the field.

papers.title: A Clinical Atlas for Phenome-Wide Association Study of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Across Electronic Health Record Domains
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a heterogeneous disorder whose associations across the entire phenome remain incompletely characterized by hypothesis-driven outcome-specific analyses. We constructed a multidomain atlas for phenome-wide association study of OSA in 222,109 adults undergoing diagnostic sleep testing in Kaiser Permanente Southern California. Using apnea-hypopnea index, we examined cross-sectional associations across diagnoses, laboratory tests, medications, procedures, healthcare utilization, behaviors, and symptoms; associations with incident diseases; and data-driven cross-domain phenotypes. After full adjustment, 169 prevalent phecodes and 16 incident phecodes remained Bonferroni-significant. Positive associations converged most consistently on cardiometabolic diseases, including hypertension, impaired glucose metabolism, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and heart failure, with concordant laboratory, medication, and cardiac-measurement signals. Multidimensional physiologic, symptom, and comorbidity phenotypes showed heterogeneous disease incidence after adjustment, with patterns not aligned with apnea-hypopnea index severity alone. These findings define the broad clinical landscape of OSA and provide a comprehensive atlas for replication and hypothesis generation.

papers.title: Faster peak alpha frequency precedes higher menstrual pain in adolescence
papers.abstract: Brain differences in chronic pain are almost always measured after years of pain experience, leaving unresolved whether they create vulnerability to pain or result from it. Uniquely, menstrual pain has a developmentally scheduled onset (menarche, the first menstrual period), allowing the brain to be characterized before and after pain exposure occurs. Here we used longitudinal 64-channel EEG to measure resting brain activity in adolescents once before (n=250) and twice after (n=161, n=140) menarche. Before their first period, adolescents who later reported higher menstrual pain (30 or greater on a 0 to 100 VAS) already showed faster occipital peak alpha frequency compared to those who reported lower menstrual pain, a difference that persisted in the early (3 to 14 months) post-menarche time period. In contrast, oscillatory power and functional connectivity did not differ by menstrual pain group, suggesting that the widespread functional brain alterations reported in adults with painful periods take years to emerge. Peak alpha frequency increased, and theta power and connectivity decreased across the menarchal transition, consistent with typical adolescent maturation. However, longitudinal analyses stratified by higher and lower menstrual pain group suggested group specific timings for these neurodevelopmental changes. Overall, these findings suggest that early menstrual pain is not associated with widespread alterations in neural oscillations, but aspects of menstrual pain susceptibility may be reflected in resting peak alpha frequency. To our knowledge, this is the first neurophysiological trait shown to precede the onset of menstrual pain.

papers.title: Cortical physiological arousal following termination of absence seizures
papers.abstract: Although the brain state preceding and during absence seizures has been well-characterized, the postictal brain state remains largely unexplored due to the prevailing assumption that absence seizures have minimal or no postictal changes. To address this gap, scalp EEG recordings from 55 patients with 3-4 Hz spike-wave discharges across four multi-site cohorts were analyzed. Spectral power was measured relative to each seizure's preictal baseline, and the postictal period was compared to a time-matched preictal window. Rather than an immediate return to baseline after seizure offset, a significant broadband increase in EEG power was observed in the gamma (>25 Hz) and delta (<4 Hz) frequency bands, followed by a gradual decline over the next 15 s to 30 s. In contrast, no comparable change preceded the seizures. This suggests that recovery from an absence seizure is an active process with a characteristic electrophysiological signature consistent with cortical activation and arousal. Thus, postictal arousal may facilitate exit from the seizure state, and with further work could serve as an electrophysiological marker and therapeutic target for recovery in absence epilepsy.

papers.title: EEG Biomarkers for Rett Syndrome: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning and Deep Learning with Explainable AI
papers.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by abnormal cortical activity, which can be captured using electroencephalography (EEG). Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise for diagnosing several neurological conditions, comprehensive evaluation of classical ML and deep learning (DL) methods, together with physiologically meaningful explanations, remains limited for RTT. This study analyses resting-state, eyes-closed EEG recordings from RTT patients and healthy controls using both power spectral density (PSD)-based ML and end-to-end DL frameworks. Classical ML models, including Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and XGBoost, were trained on PSD features, while EEG-specific DL architectures, including ShallowConvNet, DeepConvNet, EEGNet, and EEG Conformer, were trained directly on preprocessed EEG signals. Subject-wise cross-validation was used to avoid data leakage, with balanced accuracy as the primary performance metric because it equally accounts for sensitivity and specificity. Random Forest achieved the best performance among the classical ML models, whereas EEGNet achieved the highest DL performance. An ablation study indicated that 4-second EEG epochs offered the optimal trade-off between model performance and robustness. Model interpretability was investigated using SHAP for Random Forest and occlusion sensitivity analysis for EEGNet. Both methods consistently identified delta and theta oscillations, along with centro-frontal brain regions, as key contributors to RTT classification. These findings show that both PSD-based machine learning and end-to-end deep learning methods can reliably identify RTT and highlight common neurophysiological biomarkers, offering an interpretable framework for EEG-based diagnosis and biomarker discovery for Rett Syndrome.

papers.title: Insomnia and the genetic overlap of sleep with depression and anxiety: a genomic structural equation modelling study
papers.abstract: Insomnia, depression and anxiety co-occur and share genetic liability, but a genetic correlation cannot show whether that liability is spread across the sleep domain or concentrated in insomnia, a diagnostic criterion for depression and generalized anxiety disorder. We applied genomic structural equation modelling to ten genome-wide association studies and fitted a four-factor model of sleep, internalizing (depression and anxiety), psychotic-bipolar and metabolic liability. A model linking the sleep and internalizing domains only through their factor correlation was inadmissible, and we compared, under one decision rule, each one-parameter link that could repair it: domain-wide links, an insomnia-specific cross-loading, and residual covariances representing shared diagnostic content, of which three were admissible. The insomnia cross-loading fitted better than the only admissible domain-wide alternative ({Delta}AIC = 13.8; better in 98.6% of 500 Monte Carlo draws) and than shared content ({Delta}AIC = 96.9), and placing it on psychotic-bipolar or metabolic liability was inadmissible. Under this model the insomnia pathway carried 56.3% of the sleep-internalizing covariance (95% CI 45.6-67.0%). A second sleep pathway improved fit ({Delta}AIC = -33.3), but with three sleep indicators its location was not identifiable, and across the equivalent models the insomnia share ranged from 0% to 127.0%. At the variant level, no internalizing lead departed from depression-anxiety proportionality after correction, and internalizing leads replicated in FinnGen, with partial sample overlap, whereas sleep leads did not (60.4%; P = 0.17). How concentrated the overlap is will require finer sleep phenotypes to establish. Among single-link models, insomnia is the best-supported location of the overlap.

papers.title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients
papers.abstract: Background: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. Methods: We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. Results: ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). Discussion: These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

papers.title: Single-Case Design for Network-based BCI Rehabilitation: Individual Learning Trajectories and Effects of Motor Imagery Timing in Stroke Patients
papers.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are increasingly investigated for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, it remains unclear how BCI control improves through repeated training in stroke patients and whether the timing of MI decoding systematically influences this trajectory. To address this question, we implemented a single-case experimental design involving five chronic stroke patients enrolling in a longitudinal electroencephalography MI-BCI training involving their affected hand. Across 18 sessions conducted over six weeks, the onset of a fixed-duration MI decoding window was randomized to occur 1, 2, or 3~s after cue onset according to an alternating-treatments single-case design. Notably, the BCI combined spectral power and functional connectivity features to classify MI states. The MI classification timing had no significant effect on BCI accuracy, fatigue, or spasticity. BCI accuracy increased across training in four of five patients and was accompanied by patient-specific longitudinal changes in local spectral activity and functional connectivity. These convergent trajectories were consistent with acquisition of BCI control, but were not accompanied by clinically meaningful improvement in motor function. Varying the onset of the MI decoding window provided no systematic benefit for BCI control. Instead, differences in neurophysiological trajectories across patients indicate that MI decoding parameters need to be personalized and reassessed throughout the training. Overall, these findings inform more individualized and effective BCI settings for neuromotor stroke rehabilitation.

papers.title: Characterization of Sleep, Spectral, and Epileptiform Activity in Individuals Aged 8-27 Years with SYNGAP1-Related Disorder Using an at-Home Dry EEG Headband
papers.abstract: SYNGAP1-related disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is associated with sleep disturbances, seizures, and neurophysiological abnormalities. However, in-lab EEG can be difficult to obtain due to the behavioral and sensory disorders associated with this condition. In this study we collected EEG in SYNGAP1-RD participants (n=30 enrolled, 27 contributing data) in a decentralized protocol using a dry electrode headband as a path to longitudinal, research-grade data collection in this population. At-home data collection was successful with 180 recordings containing over 1 hour of usable data collected from 23 participants. Across these recordings, sporadic interictal epileptiform discharges were present in 22 of 23 participants but electrographic seizures were not observed. Relative to an adolescent control population (n=10), SYNGAP1-RD participants showed increased wake after sleep onset, reduced sleep efficiency, and decreased time in N1 and N3 sleep stages along with increased time in N2. We reproduced prior findings from awake spectral EEG analyses, including elevated broadband power along with reduced relative alpha power and alpha-theta ratio in the SYNGAP1 cohort. Notably, differences in spectral power were tightly linked to sleep stage, revealing sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics not previously characterized in SYNGAP1-RD. Finally, we examined differences between variants producing truncations downstream of the GAP domain and those producing truncations before or within it, but analyses were limited by a small sample size (n=4 for the post-GAP variant). Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of at-home multi-night sleep EEG collection in participants with SYNGAP1-RD and led to both corroborative and novel findings.
